table.text: (A, B) Schematic of a visual memory task where participants are presented with colored disks.

After a brief delay, one stimulus is either cued by its color (green disk in the center), and participants are asked to recall its location (A), or one stimulus is cued by its location (black circle), and participants are asked to report its color by selecting the corresponding point on the color wheel (B).

ethics_check.report:

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Introductory statistics courses and conventional methods in behavioral and cognitive science are typically restricted to Euclidean space without explicitly stating this, leaving many researchers unaware of how to handle data with circular or periodic properties (e.g., time of day or orientation on a screen).
This tutorial provides an accessible yet rigorous introduction, designed to bridge the gap between statistical theory and practical application.
After an overview of common applications, we discuss different ways of representing circular data mathematically and fundamental principles for working with them.
We explain angular and vector representations and operations, including key considerations for implementing them in computer code.
We then survey methods for visualizing circular data, including linear and polar plots and presentation of summary statistics.
Next, we discuss circular measures of central tendency, dispersion, and shape: how they relate to their Euclidean counterparts and why they differ.
Finally, we turn to more advanced topics of the kind needed to construct models of circular data.

We introduce the most common circular distribution families, including circular analogs of the Gaussian distribution and their properties, as well as flexible distribution families that can describe skewed and heavy-tailed data.
The tutorial takes a methodoriented approach, not tied to specific software, but highlighting factors relevant to experimental design, data analysis, and statistical modeling.
A consistent theme is the need to rigorously account for the inherent periodicity of circular data.
We also provide a consistent notation for circular statistics and parameters, addressing the lack of established conventions in the field.

Mathematical training for biological and psychological scientists typically focuses on the analysis of data in Euclidean spaces, particularly measurements that can be described as points on the real number line (referred to as R 1 ; Figure 1A), or as coordinates in a plane (R² ) or in three-dimensional space (R 3 ).
text.formatted: Mathematical training for biological and psychological scientists typically focuses on the analysis of data in Euclidean spaces, particularly measurements that can be described as points on the real number line (referred to as R 1 ; Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>), or as coordinates in a plane (R² ) or in three-dimensional space (R 3 ).

text.text: However, many biological and behavioral variables have a periodic or cyclical nature that requires different methods of analysis.

Measurements in a circular space (denoted S 1 ) can be described by a single number (as on the real line), but moving far enough through the value range in either direction returns you to the point where you started (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: Measurements in a circular space (denoted S 1 ) can be described by a single number (as on the real line), but moving far enough through the value range in either direction returns you to the point where you started (Figure <ref type="figure">1B</ref>).

text.text: Such a space is topologically equivalent to a closed loop or circle and fundamentally different from the real line (which stretches to infinity in either direction) or a bounded interval (a section of the real line with two ends).

A simple example of a circular space is the directions of a compass: If you describe directions in terms of angles (e.g., measured clockwise from North), then 0 • , 360 • and 720 • all refer to the same direction, and the distance between 0 • and 359 • is the same as the distance between 0 • and 1 • .
The topic of circular statistics describes methods for analyzing random variables in circular spaces.

It is a subset of directional statistics, which extends to variables that can be represented as points on a sphere (S 2 , which includes directions in threedimensional space), and analogs in higher dimensions.
This tutorial focuses on methods for circular data, as they are widely applicable to behavioral research and also provide a foundation for learning about directional statistics more generally.
For an introduction to higher-dimensional directional statistics, refer to Mardia and Jupp (2009) and Pewsey and García-Portugués (2021).

text.text: This tutorial targets researchers who are familiar with statistical measures and distributions in Euclidean space and want to understand the corresponding circular equivalents.

It develops progressively, from the basic properties and operations needed to present and analyze circular data to more advanced concepts, including the foundations for formal generative models that output circular variables.
Conventions for mathematical notation in circular statistics are less standardized than in Euclidean statistics.

In cases where there is a strong convention, we have followed it, but for cases where there is not, we have developed a notation (Table 1 and Appendix A) that aims to be clear and self-consistent, although it should not be regarded as canonical.

text.text: We will begin with a survey of use cases for circular statistics in behavioral and cognitive research (Section Applications).

This section gives an overview of the wide range of applications of circular statistics; the publications cited in this section may also help orient the reader to how circular statistics can be applied to specific topics and types of data.

In Section Working With Circular Data, we will introduce key characteristics of circular data, different ways of conceptualizing circular values and describing them numerically, and elementary operations on circular variables.
Section Visualizations of Circular Data gives an overview of different options for visualizing circular data and the methodology behind them.

Section Descriptive Statistics of Circular Data will cover the most important statistical measures for circular data, including analogs of mean and variance, and why they differ from their better-known Euclidean counterparts.

We will then explore circular statistical models (Section Probability Theory and Models for Circular Variables), including the vexed question of circular equivalents to the normal distribution, and concepts of importance to constructing ideal observer and Bayesian models.

We will conclude with an overview of further topics in circular statistics that fall outside the scope of this tutorial, providing references to the most useful sources (Section Beyond This Tutorial).
text.formatted: We will conclude with an overview of further topics in circular statistics that fall outside the scope of this tutorial, providing references to the most useful sources <ref type="bibr">(Section Beyond This Tutorial)</ref>.

text.text: Many areas of behavioral and cognitive research involve data that are either inherently circular or benefit from being conceptualized as circular in order to design experiments or analyze data.
To illustrate its broad practical relevance, this section presents use cases of circular statistics, including for spatial, temporal, and neural data.
Circular statistics can be a valuable tool for behavioral research using spatial data.

Many aspects of spatial cognition and behavior naturally involve circular variables, while in other cases spatial features that are not inherently circular may be constrained to a circular subspace for purposes of experiment or analysis.
In the following, we will look at examples of both.
As described in the introduction, compass direction is an inherently circular spatial feature, with animal navigation and migration as a classic use case.

Factors supporting navigation include the relative direction of the sun (Giraldo et al., 2018; Lindecke et al., 2019), moonlight and stars (Foster et al., 2019; Freas et al., 2024), and, in some animals, the orientation of magnetic fields (Packmor et al., 2024; Panagopoulos et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Factors supporting navigation include the relative direction of the sun <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Giraldo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Lindecke et al., 2019)</ref>, moonlight and stars <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Foster et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Freas et al., 2024)</ref>, and, in some animals, the orientation of magnetic fields <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Packmor et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Panagopoulos et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Circular statistics have been used to study movement directions in migration routes of birds (Bolón et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024; Packmor et al., 2024), insects (Huang et al., 2024; Vijayan & Somanathan, 2024), and mammals (Thompson et al., 2024).

text.text: Circular statistics have also been employed to study movement patterns on smaller scales, such as bee waggle dances.

This complex form of non-verbal, symbolic communication allows forager bees to inform each other about food sources: the angle of the waggle run relative to gravity encodes the angle of the food source in relation to the sun.
Circular statistics allow for an appropriate analysis of these complex dances (Deverell, 2003; Schürch & Couvillon, 2013; Vijayan & Somanathan, 2024).

text.text: Location in space is an example of a feature that, although not circular by nature, may be structured circularly to support experimental design.
In human vision research, for instance, it is common to record responses of experimental participants to visual stimuli presented via a computer display.

If stimuli were presented at random locations across the whole display, differences in their retinal eccentricity (distance of the image from the central foveal region of the retina) would influence how they are processed by the visual system (Olivers, 2025; Staugaard et al., 2016).

text.text: Additionally, the stimuli's varying proximity to the borders of the screen could influence how they are perceived (Fortenbaugh et al., 2012; May & Zhaoping, 2009; Schulz-Hildebrandt, 2025).

text.text: Human and animal behavior is often structured in recurring patterns, many of which follow approximately or exactly repeating cycles.
Some of these cycles have a biological basis (e.g., hormonal rhythms), while others are shaped by environmental factors or, in humans, by cultural conventions (e.g., weekly schedules).
Often, biological and cultural factors jointly determine how humans experience time and its influence on behavior (Patke et al., 2020).

text.text: A key feature for classifying and distinguishing periodic systems is the length of a single cycle.
The most commonly studied chronobiological rhythm is the circadian rhythm (from Latin circa -approximately, dies -day), which has a period of about 24 hours.
Numerous physiological and behavioral processes in humans and other animals vary systematically across the day.

Among others, circadian rhythms influence sleep-wake cycles (Saper et al., 2005; Zisapel, 2018), hormone secretion (Nelson et al., 2025; Zisapel, 2018), body temperature (Refinetti, 2020), and activity patterns (Lautenschlager et al., 2024; Palmeirim et al., 2025).

text.text: Through electrophysiological recordings in V1 in cats and monkeys, they identified neurons that were selectively responsive to specific orientations of a visible bar or grating presented on a flat screen.

Each cell had a "preferred" orientation that caused it to be most active (Figure 4A), and neurons with similar orientation preferences were grouped into vertical columns (Hubel & Wiesel, 1962 , 1968; Hubel et al., 1977).

text.text: These orientation columns form orderly, repeating patterns across the cortical surface, often described as "pinwheels", because preferred orientations of neurons rotate continuously around a central point, covering the full range of orientations (Blasdel & Salama, 1986; Bonhoeffer & Grinvald, 1991; Bonhoeffer et al., 1995; Maldonado et al., 1997; Ts'o et al., 1990).

text.text: They investigated the activity of neurons in the primary motor cortex (M1) of monkeys making reaching movements in the horizontal plane.
They found neurons whose firing rate varied as an approximately cosine function of movement direction, each with a preferred direction that induced maximum activity.

By treating each neuron's instantaneous firing rate as the length of a vector pointing in its preferred direction, and summing across all neurons, they obtained a "population" vector whose direction closely matched the actual reach direction on that trial.

text.text: Most examples we discussed above reflect physical measurements of time or space that have a circular or periodic structure.
However, there are also more abstract perceptual, cognitive, and behavioral variables for which a circular representation is appropriate or has proven useful.
For instance, circular statistics have been employed in social psychology to examine interpersonal interactions.

This includes the synchronization of body movements to those of an interaction partner (Koul et al., 2023; Macpherson et al., 2024), interactions in romantic relationships (Sadikaj et al., 2015; Vowels et al., 2018), and interpersonal behavior of teachers (Cremers et al., 2021; van der Lans et al., 2020).

Together, these two dimensions form a circular space in which interpersonal behaviors are located as angles on a circle (Gurtman, 2009; Leary, 1957; Wiggins, 1991).

In this section, we describe the fundamental characteristics of circular data to provide the foundation for subsequent sections.

We explain the advantages of describing circular values as vectors of unit length in a two-dimensional plane and three standard forms of this vector representation: in polar coordinates, Cartesian coordinates, and on the complex plane.
There is no universally correct choice for representing a given circular dataset; the optimal representation depends on the context and purpose of the analysis.
For instance, angular measurements are often more intuitive for data visualization.
If the methods described here are correctly applied, conclusions drawn from circular data will remain valid regardless of the chosen representation.
Finding the appropriate cycle length requires careful consideration, as an unsuitable choice might bias results.
One cycle needs to contain every distinct point in the space of possible data values exactly once.
Points that are separated by a whole number of cycles must be identical or at least equivalent for the purpose of the analysis.

Selecting too narrow a period risks obscuring important aspects of the data by treating data points as equivalent when they are not: For instance, if temporal data are analyzed on a daily level, but they actually displays weekly rhythms.

On the other hand, selecting too wide a period will mean the periodic nature of the data is not properly accounted for. Liu and West (2016) discuss a method for identifying an appropriate cycle length for circular analysis of temporal data.

text.text: Having identified the periodicity of our circular data, we can map each observation to its corresponding angle or phase, indicating where it falls within one full period or cycle.
This requires us to select a data value that will correspond to an angle of 0, and a direction in the data space that will correspond to the positive direction of increasing angle.

In some cases these choices are obvious (e.g., for temporal data with a period of one day, one would usually assign 12 o'clock midnight to the zero angle and increasing positive angular values to later times in the day), but in others they may be arbitrary, or the researcher may have to choose between several viable alternatives.
Angles are typically measured in degrees ( • ), in which case one cycle covers a range of 360 • , or radians (rad), in which case (for reasons explained below) one cycle covers 2𝜋 (≈ 6.28) rad.
As discussed above, for data consisting of directions or orientations in space, the angular units of the circular space may differ from those of the raw data.
The units in which angular values are reported are a matter of choice, subject to conventions of the field, but some mathematical operations are simplified by using radians.
To convert an angle in degrees to radians, multiply by the ratio 𝜋 180 , and divide by the same ratio to convert the other way.

Similarly, uppercase Greek letters -Θ (Theta), Φ (Phi), or Ψ (Psi) -are often used for sets or collections of elements analogous to 𝑋 or 𝑌 in Euclidean space.

However, for many of the calculations we will want to perform on circular data, a vector representation (i.e., one combining angle and distance) turns out to be even more powerful.
There are three mathematically equivalent ways to represent such a vector, summarized in Figure 7, and each offers distinct advantages depending on the context of application.

text.text: Representing a circular value in polar coordinates simply involves supplementing the angular representation of data, 𝜃, with a distance or norm, 𝑟, resulting in the polar coordinate pair (𝑟, 𝜃).
By convention the norm is set to 1, giving (1, 𝜃).

Now each observation is identified not just with a direction but also with a specific point in the two-dimensional plane, and the space of all possible observations is described by a circle of unit radius.
Technically, this is an embedding of the circular space (S 1 ) in the real plane (R² ).

We can now appreciate the basis for radian units: an angle of 𝑋 rad corresponds to a distance 𝑋 measured on the circumference of the circle, with a full period corresponding to the full circumference of 2𝜋.

text.text: We can also describe circular observations as vectors in a Cartesian coordinate system, with origin 𝑂 and two perpendicular axes, 𝑋 and 𝑌 , passing through 𝑂.
By convention, the 0 • direction is positive on the 𝑥-axis.
In this reference frame, any point on the plane can be represented as a pair of rectangular coordinates [𝑥, 𝑦], with unit vectors constrained to have 𝑥 2 + 𝑦2 = 1.
Compared with a polar representation, this simplifies vector operations (which are used to define statistics like the circular mean; see Section Descriptive Statistics of Circular Data).
For example, addition of two vectors simply involves pairwise addition of their Cartesian coordinates.
On the other hand, it makes angular operations, such as adding two angles together, more difficult.
The Cartesian vector representation is the most easily extended to higher-dimensional directional statistics.
For example, spherical data can be represented by unit vectors in three dimensions, described in [𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧] coordinates.

text.text: As described above, the defining characteristic of circular data is its inherent periodicity, meaning that measurements that differ by a whole number of cycles are considered equivalent.
This property fundamentally distinguishes circular from Euclidean space, where proximity and ordering follow conventional numerical relationships.
For example, in Euclidean space, 1 is always closer to 3 than 10.
In circular spaces, values that may appear numerically distant can in fact be close, for example, 1 • and 359 • differ by only 2 • because 1 • and 361 • are equivalent angles.

While conceptually any observation in a circular space can be represented by infinitely many angular values, differing by whole numbers of cycles, for practical purposes, it is usually constrained to one unique value within a specific periodic interval.
According to the mathematical convention, angular values are constrained to a positive interval [0, 2𝜋) rad.
Note that the square bracket indicates the inclusion of the lower bound and the round bracket the exclusion of the upper bound.
This specification ensures that the same point is not included twice, which would occur if both bounds were closed, that is, with this definition, an observation can be assigned to 0 but not 2𝜋.

The term "wrapping" is often used for the process of mapping circular observations to their representative values within a specified interval (imagine wrapping the real number line around the unit circle, like winding thread onto a bobbin).

The process of wrapping angle 𝜃 to the interval [0, 2𝜋) can be described by a modulo operation, where 𝑎 mod 𝑏 is the least nonnegative residue of 𝑎 modulo 𝑏, that is, the smallest number ≥ 0 that can be obtained by subtracting an integer multiple of 𝑏 from 𝑎.

When working with Euclidean variables, there exist many operations that map real numbers to other real numbers.

By contrast, for circular variables, the need to respect periodic equivalence means there are very few operations that map angles to other angles: Essentially, these are limited to addition, subtraction, and multiplication by integer quantities (equivalent to repeated addition or subtraction).
While it is possible to perform other operations on numerical representations of angles, the results will depend on the particular interval you have chosen for representation.
For instance, 0 • and 360 • refer to the same angle, but if you attempt to divide them by 2 you will get 0 • and 180 • , which are different angles.
Having specified a range of angles in which to represent circular data, we will want to represent the results of angular addition and subtraction within the same interval.
Practically, this just means applying a "wrapping" or modulo operation, as described above, after the usual arithmetic operation of addition or subtraction.
A familiar example of modular arithmetic is the hour hand on a clock dial.
If we subtract 2 hours from 1 o'clock, we get 11 o'clock, not -1 o'clock.
Similarly, if we add 5 hours to 10 o'clock, we get 3 o'clock and not 15 o'clock.

Modular subtraction can be used to recenter data on a particular reference direction, or compute the angular deviation or error of an estimate 𝜃 from a true value 𝜙.

text.text: In Cartesian coordinates, rotation of vectors is achieved by multiplying by a rotation matrix.
A rotation of a vector with coordinates [𝑥, 𝑦] through an angle 𝜙 about the origin 𝑂 can be expressed in matrix form as:
The rotation is counterclockwise in standard coordinates if 𝜙 is positive, and clockwise if it is negative.
If [𝑥, 𝑦] is a unit vector corresponding to angle 𝜃, then [𝑥 ′ , 𝑦 ′ ] is another unit vector corresponding to angle 𝜃 + 𝜙.

Rotation matrices are a relatively cumbersome way of implementing angular arithmetic, but they find considerable application in computer graphics, including 3D graphics where rotations in three dimensions are expressed analogously as 3×3 matrices.

Importantly, in computer graphics software, pixel locations on a two-dimensional display are usually represented in a nonstandard "left-handed" Cartesian system, with 𝑦 increasing downward instead of upward, 𝑥 increasing to the right, and the origin at the top-left corner of the display.
In this system, all coordinates lie in the first quadrant where 𝑥 ≥ 0 and 𝑦 ≥ 0.
The inversion of the 𝑦-axis reverses the sense of rotation, so for screen coordinates [𝑥, 𝑦], the rotation described by Equation 11 is clockwise for positive 𝜃.
For circular values represented as unit vectors in the complex plane, the addition and subtraction of angles correspond to multiplication and division, respectively.
That is, if 𝑧 1 and 𝑧 2 are two unit complex numbers corresponding to the angles 𝜃 and 𝜙, then their product is yielding a new unit vector representing the angle 𝜃 + 𝜙.
Similarly, the subtraction 𝜃 -𝜙 corresponds to dividing the vector representation of 𝜃 by the vector representation of 𝜙:

The complex representation therefore provides a simple and mathematically elegant implementation of angular arithmetic, in which the "wrapping around" of large angle changes is taken care of automatically by the geometry of the complex plane.

Many programming languages have support for complex numbers built-in (e.g., in both MATLAB and Python you can create complex numbers by typing 1j for the imaginary unit i and they will work with all the usual math operators and functions), whereas other languages have well-established libraries that implement them (e.g., math.js for JavaScript).

Note, however, that the complex representation of circular variables does not have convenient extensions to spherical or higher-dimensional directional variables: The polar and Cartesian representations provide better starting points for working with those kinds of data.
The periodic equivalence of circular data means careful consideration must be given to the measurement of distances.
The Euclidean distance between two points on the real number line is just the absolute value of their difference, calculated equivalently as either |𝑥 -𝑦| or |𝑦 -𝑥|.

By contrast, given two angles 𝜃 and 𝜙 corresponding to two points 𝐴 and 𝐵 on the unit circle, their angular separation can be measured either clockwise or counterclockwise, yielding two different distances that add up to one complete cycle.
The angular distance is typically taken as the smaller of the two, equivalent to the shortest arc length between 𝐴 and 𝐵 (Figures 8C and 8D).

The resulting distance always lies in [0, 𝜋] and it captures the magnitude of the angular separation, without regard to its direction.
Note that the angular distance is not itself a circular variable.

The cosine dissimilarity lies in the range [0, 2], with 0 and 2 corresponding to the minimum and maximum possible separation of 0 and 𝜋 rad, respectively.

This measure of distance can be conceptualized as a circular analogue of the squared Euclidean distance and plays a similarly important role in circular statistics, including in the definition of circular variance, as we will discuss in Section Circular Variance.

Indeed, with respect to the vector representation of angles, the cosine dissimilarity is equal to half the squared straight-line distance between points on the unit circle, that is, 1 2 ||A -B|| 2 in the Cartesian representation or 1 2 |𝑧 1 -𝑧 2 | 2 in the complex representation.
For unit vectors with small differences in angle 𝛿, the straight-line distance and the angular distance are approximately equal, so the cosine dissimilarity 1cos(𝛿) converges to 𝛿 2 2 .
Note that, like angular distance, the cosine dissimilarity is not a circular variable.
In study design, circular distance becomes relevant when a minimum or maximum separation between angular values must be ensured.
Such constraints allow continuous rather than discrete variables while keeping points neither too close nor too far apart.

For instance, experimental stimuli could be sampled with a minimum circular distance so they remain perceptually distinct, or ambulatory-assessment surveys scheduled at random times subject to a maximum gap between them.
A method for sampling from a uniform distribution in circular space while ensuring a minimum separation between values is provided in Appendix C.

text.text: Visualizing circular data requires approaches that respect its inherent periodicity and directional nature.

A key decision to make is whether data are unwrapped onto a line and represented in a Euclidean coordinate system or represented in a two-dimensional polar coordinate system -where angle is mapped to direction (𝜃) and magnitude to radius (𝑟).
In some cases, linear and polar visualizations convey similar information, whereas in others, one format provides a much clearer or more intuitive representation of the data.
This section will outline common approaches and potential pitfalls in the visualization of circular data, concluding with a discussion of methods for visualizing summary statistics.
We also provide practical guidance on producing these visualizations in commonly used programming languages.

One common way to visualize circular data is by unwrapping it into a linear histogram along the circular dimension, using binned counts (absolute or relative frequencies) or continuous density estimates.
This requires two key decisions: selecting the interval and -as for Euclidean data -defining the bins.
Both the standard interval [0, 2𝜋) and the signed interval [-𝜋, 𝜋), are common choices for linear visualizations.
The latter is especially useful if there is a meaningful zero point, such as for errors relative to a reference angle.
The choice of the interval determines the wrap-around point, which critically affects how clearly the structure of the data is displayed.
When data are unimodal and highly concentrated, a linear histogram can closely resemble a standard histogram of non-circular data and often provides a simple, interpretable summary.
In such cases, the interval should be chosen so that the region of highest density lies in the center of the 𝑥-axis.
For multimodal distributions, boundaries should, where possible, be positioned in regions of low density to ensure that all modes are clearly represented.

For instance, in Figure 9A, the shape of the distribution around the dominant mode is clearly presented, while the secondary mode is positioned too close to the boundary, leading to density spilling over to the opposite side of the plot.

text.text: As for Euclidean data, the choice of bin size further shapes the appearance of the histogram: wider bins "smooth" over noise but may conceal fine structure in the data, whereas narrower bins reveal more detail but are susceptible to spurious fluctuations (Figure 9B).

text.text: However, heuristics based on dispersion measures may perform poorly in circular space and even yield pathological results, such as vanishing bin widths for near-uniform data.
Currently, no universally accepted bin-selection rule exists for circular histograms.
In practice, researchers often use a fixed number of bins.
Crucially, bin widths and locations should be selected so that edges coincide with the boundaries of the presentation interval.

Another consequence of mapping circular data to a linear axis is that subgroup visualization no longer requires any circular-specific treatment; the same methods used for Euclidean data apply directly, including grouped, overlaid, or stacked histograms (e.g., Figure 9I).

text.text: A related method is to plot a linear continuous density curve, which provides a smoothed representation of the distribution.
For sufficiently dense data, continuous density curves intuitively summarize the overall structure of the distribution without being tied to arbitrary bin edges.

However, as for bin size in histograms, the choice of smoothing parameter strongly influences the result: too much smoothing can mask structure, while too little smoothing exaggerates noise (Figure 9C).
text.formatted: However, as for bin size in histograms, the choice of smoothing parameter strongly influences the result: too much smoothing can mask structure, while too little smoothing exaggerates noise (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">9C</ref>).

text.text: Additionally, a smoothing algorithm that takes into account the connectedness of the two ends of the interval must be chosen.
As for the Euclidean case, circular continuous density plots are not appropriate for discrete or heavily rounded data or for sparse data, where density estimates can be unstable or misleading.
For a short review of nonparametric methods for smooth density estimation of circular data, see Chaubey (2022).
text.formatted: For a short review of nonparametric methods for smooth density estimation of circular data, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Chaubey (2022)</ref>.

text.text: The empirical cumulative distribution function (eCDF) summarizes the data without requiring a choice of bin size or smoothing parameter (Figure 9D).
text.formatted: The empirical cumulative distribution function (eCDF) summarizes the data without requiring a choice of bin size or smoothing parameter (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">9D</ref>).

text.text: It shows the cumulative proportion of observations along the circular axis and can help highlight changes in density while avoiding some of the visual noise of histograms.

Like other linear representations, however, eCDFs still require choosing an interval, and selecting the interval so that the wrap-around point lies opposite the region of highest concentration helps to center the distribution.
For producing linear plots of circular data, readers can use the same software and functions familiar from visualizing Euclidean data.

For this, it is essential that the data are correctly wrapped (i.e., mapped to their representative values within the interval selected for visualization), and if applicable, that density estimation is conducted using methods accounting for the periodicity of the data.
Once the circular data are appropriately preprocessed, linear plots can be generated by using the same software for (binning and) plotting as for Euclidean data.

We saw that linear visualizations such as histograms and eCDFs are intuitive and effective for concentrated, unimodal data.
However, they may obscure structure in more dispersed or multimodal distributions, especially near wrap-around points.
In such cases, polar visualizations often provide a clearer representation.
Polar histograms are widely used for polar representation of circular data (Figures 9E and 9F).

text.text: The rose plot is a type of polar histogram that represents frequency data as radial wedges of equal angular width radiating from the center of a circle (Figure 9E).
text.formatted: The rose plot is a type of polar histogram that represents frequency data as radial wedges of equal angular width radiating from the center of a circle (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">9E</ref>).

text.text: The height of each wedge indicates the number or proportion of observations in that angular bin.
Unlike linear histograms, this approach preserves the continuity of the circular scale and avoids edge artifacts introduced by unwrapping.
It also makes features such as the central tendency and directional biases easier to see.
However, the representation is still influenced by the choice of bin size and the placement of the bin edges (for an illustration, see Figure 1 in Wells, 2000).

text.text: Analogous to its linear equivalent, a polar continuous density curve maps the smoothed density around the circle (Figures 9G and 9H).
This representation conveys the same information as the linear density plot but emphasizes the cyclical structure of the data and does not require choosing a wraparound point.

As before, the choice of smoothing parameter strongly influences the result, and continuous density plots are also unsuitable for sparse data and data rounded to a coarse resolution, where density estimates can become unstable.
A key consideration in polar representations is how magnitude is mapped to radial distance.

Because the area of a polar region (i.e., a wedge or the area under a smooth curve) grows with the square of its radius, mapping frequency or density directly to radial height causes area to scale quadratically (Figure 9G).
text.formatted: Because the area of a polar region (i.e., a wedge or the area under a smooth curve) grows with the square of its radius, mapping frequency or density directly to radial height causes area to scale quadratically (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">9G</ref>).

text.text: This distorts the apparent magnitude because small differences in height translate into large differences in area.
As a result, dense regions are spatially overrepresented, while sparse areas are understated and difficult to distinguish.
The problem arises for both binned counts and smooth densities.
To correct this, radial height can be mapped to the square root of frequency or density (Mardia & Jupp, 2009).
text.formatted: To correct this, radial height can be mapped to the square root of frequency or density <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Mardia & Jupp, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This ensures that the area of each sector is linearly proportional to the actual quantity, making sector areas directly comparable across angles.

However, this comes at the cost of interpretability of the radial axis: because radial distance now represents the square root of frequency or density, values can no longer be read directly from the radius.

text.text: A version of polar histograms that avoids a distorted representation of area is wrapped bar histograms, which use rectangular bars arranged around a reference circle instead of wedges (Figure 9F).
text.formatted: A version of polar histograms that avoids a distorted representation of area is wrapped bar histograms, which use rectangular bars arranged around a reference circle instead of wedges (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">9F</ref>).

text.text: The base of each bar is aligned with the reference circle's circumference, and the radius of the reference circle is set arbitrarily to ensure that the bars fit around its perimeter.
This method effectively wraps a linear histogram around a circle, preserving the height of each bar relative to its linear counterpart.
This approach avoids the distortions of apparent magnitude typical of wedge-based rose plots, because both height and area are proportional to frequency.

However, the gaps between adjacent bars complicate overlaying smooth density curves: to remain consistent with bar heights, density must be mapped to height rather than area; as a result, area under the density curve can misrepresent magnitude, with a disproportionately larger area plotted around longer bars compared to shorter bars.
For a more detailed discussion of polar histograms and their design considerations, see Sanderson and Peacock (2020).
text.formatted: For a more detailed discussion of polar histograms and their design considerations, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Sanderson and Peacock (2020)</ref>.

text.text: Stacked polar histograms (Figure 9I) can be used to show subgroup compositions within each angular bin.
text.formatted: Stacked polar histograms (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">9I</ref>) can be used to show subgroup compositions within each angular bin.

text.text: Annular sectors corresponding to different groups are layered radially one on top of another.
However, this design inherits the same distortion mentioned previously: subgroups farther from the center occupy disproportionately more area, even when counts are equal.
This occurs because area increases with the square of the radial distance, so visually comparing sector sizes can give a misleading impression of the underlying proportions.

Stacked linear histograms show subgroup magnitudes in a clearer way (Figure 9J), even though the stacked representation still makes it difficult to compare the same subgroup across bins or relative subgroup contributions within a bin.

text.text: For these comparisons, alternatives such as grouped polar bars, unstacked linear histograms, or proportion-normalized plots provide more reliable summaries.

text.text: Data consisting of paired circular and linear variables is referred to as cylindrical.
Examples include the pairing of movement direction and amplitude, and pairs of visual features like edge orientation and spatial frequency.
One way of visualizing cylindrical data is a polar scatter plot, where each point is positioned according to its angle around the circle and its distance from the center (Figure 9K).

text.text: For large datasets or continuous variables, scatter plots can become cluttered and difficult to interpret.
In these cases, polar heatmaps offer a useful alternative (Figure 9L).

text.text: Such plots summarize data density or intensity smoothly across both the circular and radial dimensions, making it easier to identify patterns in the data.
Cylindrical data can also be represented using twodimensional Cartesian plots, where one axis corresponds to one period of the circular data displayed in linear form.

text.text: While histograms and density plots illustrate the overall distribution of data, visualizations of summary statistics convey key properties, such as the dominant direction in the data or how strongly clustered the observations are.
Some of the concepts that we will introduce in this subsection (e.g., mean vector and circular median) are explained in greater detail in the https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/5n64t section.

text.text: For now, the focus is on how these statistical summaries can be effectively represented in visual form, rather than on details of their calculation.
Rayleigh plots (Figure 10A and 10B) provide a simple and informative way to visualize both individual data points and summary statistics in a single plot.

text.text: They are related to circular histograms but -in addition to individual observationsalso visually summarize central tendency and spread.
Instead of grouping observations into bins, Rayleigh plots represent each data point as a mark positioned at its corresponding angle on the circumference (Figure 10A).

text.text: While typically used for ungrouped data, Rayleigh plots can be adapted for grouped data.
In such cases, or when multiple observations share the same angle, instead of being overlaid, points can be stacked radially to show frequency (Figure 10B).

text.text: Stacking points makes individual observations easier to distinguish compared to the classic Rayleigh plot, where overlapping points can obscure one another.
A distinctive feature of the Rayleigh plot is the mean vector, drawn as an arrow from the center of the circle.
The angle of this arrow indicates the direction of central tendency, while its length reflects the spread of the data.
Thus, it provides an intuitive summary of both the main direction and the consistency of observations around it.
For a more detailed mathematical definition of the mean vector, see the https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/5n64t section.

text.text: For Euclidean data, a box plot typically displays lower quartile (Q1), median, upper quartile (Q3), with additional elements indicating the spread beyond the quartiles and potential outliers.
Circular box plots (Figure 10C and 10D) aim to represent similar features but face unique challenges due to the periodic nature of angular data.

text.text: A critical challenge is that, in circular space, the median and quartiles are not always uniquely defined, particularly in multimodal or uniform distributions (see the https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/5n64t section).

text.text: If these order statistics are not uniquely defined, a circular box plot cannot be uniquely defined either.

Despite this limitation, various implementations attempt to visualize the angular spread and central range using arcs or radial sectors to represent interquartile ranges, with additional markers for extreme values when identifiable.
Like other visualizations of circular data, circular box plots can be displayed either on a circular (Figure 10C) or linear scale (Figure 10D).

text.text: The circular format can be particularly useful for comparing multiple circular variables or groups, where box plots are positioned at increasing radii.
However, comparing such box plots can be misleading: box plots plotted farther from the origin will be physically longer than those closer in, even if their angular spreads are identical.
This can distort the perceived variability and exaggerate or diminish differences between groups.
In the example shown in Figure 10C and 10D, the three groups appear more different in terms of spread when displayed on a circular plot compared to a linear one.
text.formatted: In the example shown in Figure <ref type="figure">10C</ref> and 10D, the three groups appear more different in terms of spread when displayed on a circular plot compared to a linear one.

text.text: To support interpretation, circular box plots can include radial grid lines and concentric circles, which serve as visual reference points for comparing angular spread and position across groups plotted at different radii.

The implementation of Rayleigh plots follows the same approach as described for polar scatter plots, with the radius of each point fixed to a constant value for ungrouped data or incremented radially for each observation sharing the same angle for grouped data.

The mean vector can be added as an arrow using quiver in MATLAB, annotate with arrowprops in matplotlib in Python, and geom_segment() in ggplot2 in R. For a more detailed discussion of possible ways to implement circular box plots, refer to Abuzaid et al. (2012) and Buttarazzi et al. (2018).

Where applicable, we will also discuss the circumstances under which Euclidean approximations of circular measures provide acceptable accuracy.
As mentioned in the introduction, mathematical notation in circular statistics is less standardized than in Euclidean contexts.

A basic requirement of any statistic calculated from circular data is that it respects the equivalence of angles separated by a whole number of cycles, for example, that it is unchanged if we describe a data point as 360 • instead of 0 • .
The usual definition of the arithmetic mean 1 𝑛 ∑︁ 𝑛 𝑖=1 𝑥 𝑖 does not fulfill this requirement.
However, the problem of identifying a circular counterpart to the Euclidean mean turns out to be even more fundamental in nature.
Consider a data sample consisting of the four cardinal directions (0 • , 90 • , 180 • , and 270 • ).
Intuitively, no single direction can be identified as its average.
It is clear that a different conception of mean value is required for circular data: the centroid, or center of mass, fulfills the requirements.
In Euclidean space, the arithmetic mean is equivalent to the centroid of the set of points 𝑥 𝑖 on the real number line.

This idea can be illustrated using the analogy of a seesaw: Placing equally weighted balls at each location 𝑥 𝑖 on a beam, the mean corresponds to the center of mass, or the position of a fulcrum that balances the system.
We can extend this concept to circular data by treating each angle 𝜃 𝑖 as a point on the unit circle (the embedded representation introduced in Section Polar Coordinates).
In this case, the centroid lies inside the circle rather than on its circumference (purple dots in Figure 11).

text.text: The analogy is to a disk with equally weighted balls placed along its edge at angles 𝜃 𝑖 .
Placing a small plinth underneath the disk to keep it balanced would require positioning it closer to the center and not on the edge.
The position of the plinth reflects the location of the center of mass.
The direction of the center of mass from the origin defines the circular mean -a generalization of the linear mean that respects the periodic and directional nature of circular data.
It is the same as the direction of the resultant vector (the sum of the 𝑛 unit vectors corresponding to the data; see Section Vector Summation).

The circular mean θ is the angle that maximizes the sum of cosines of angular distances between each data point and that angle:
Equivalently, we can say it is the angle with the minimum summed cosine dissimilarity from the data (see Section Measuring Distance).

In the special case that data points are concentrated in a small region of the circular space, some (but not all) circular statistics can be approximated by their Euclidean counterparts.

In this case, the Euclidean mean will closely approximate the circular mean.

As a trivial example, for any odd number of data points arranged evenly around the circle, every data point has an equal claim to be the circular median.

The circular median is less sensitive to extreme observations or outliers than the circular mean, and can provide a robust measure of central tendency, similarly to the median versus the arithmetic mean in Euclidean space (see Section Outlier Classification and Exclusion).
When most data points are clustered in a small region in the interior of an interval of 2𝜋, the circular median is approximately equal to the Euclidean median calculated over that interval.
The circular mode of a sample is the most frequently occurring angle, taking into account the equivalence of angles separated by whole numbers of cycles.

As in the Euclidean case, the circular mode is strictly only defined for discrete data, but the term may also be used in a looser sense to describe peaks in a histogram or smoothed density estimates of continuous data.

Whereas the global mode is rarely used to estimate central tendency for continuous circular data, local mode estimates are relevant for several applications, including multimodality testing (Ameijeiras-Alonso et al., 2019; Bolón et al., 2025) and mode-based clustering approaches (Chang-Chien et al., 2012; Y. Zhang & Chen, 2021).

The sample circular variance is defined as reflecting the inverse relationship between R and spread.

The circular variance is equal to the average cosine dissimilarity between the data points and their circular mean, in the same way that the Euclidean variance is the average squared deviation from the arithmetic mean.
Unlike many other circular statistics, the circular variance of clustered data is not approximately equal to the corresponding Euclidean measure.
Instead, for data that are concentrated within a small arc of the circle, circular variance is approximately half the value of the Euclidean sample variance (red dashed line in Figure 12C).

However, applying this transformation to the circular variance, which takes values in [0, 1], would not yield a measure of spread in radians or any other natural angular units.

This definition might seem arbitrary and a bit peculiar, but it has a logic based on the Gaussian or normal distribution.

Specifically, if you wrap a Gaussian probability distribution with standard deviation 𝜎 around the unit circle (Section Wrapped Normal Distribution), the resulting distribution will have a circular standard deviation equal to 𝜎, based on this definition.
In other words, 𝑠 𝜃 is the standard deviation of a normal distribution wrapped around the circle that has the same mean resultant length as the data.

To calculate circular mean, variance, and standard deviation, we used the mean resultant vector, which can also be characterized as the first circular moment of the data distribution.
Circular moments, also called trigonometric moments, form an important class of summary statistics.
They act as a "fingerprint" of the distribution, allowing complex patterns to be summarized by a few interpretable numbers.
In Euclidean statistics, the 𝑝-th moment of the sample distribution is the arithmetic mean of the 𝑝-th power of the data values, 1 𝑛 ∑︁ 𝑖 𝑥 𝑝 𝑖 .
However, this definition does not transfer directly to circular data, because it ignores periodicity and directionality.
To properly capture the geometry of the circle, powers of 𝜃 are replaced with powers of the complex exponential 𝑒 i𝜃 = cos 𝜃 +i sin 𝜃, which is periodic with period 2𝜋.
The 𝑝-th sample circular moment is therefore defined as

The first circular moment, ˆ︁ 𝑚 1 , is the mean resultant vector (Section Circular Mean), its modulus | ˆ︁ 𝑚 1 | is the mean resultant length R, and its argument or phase arg( ˆ︁ 𝑚 1 ) is the circular mean θ.
More generally, the modulus and argument of each circular moment ˆ︁ 𝑚 𝑝 yield interesting statistics.
The argument of the p-th circular moment, corresponds to the mean direction of the data when considered modulo 2 𝜋 𝑝 , that is, when directions separated by 2 𝜋 𝑝 are treated as equivalent.
Higher-order moment arguments generalize the circular mean to capture dominant symmetries in circular data.
For instance, θ2 gives the dominant axis when opposite directions are treated as equivalent, whereas θ3 points to the orientation of a threefold (trimodal) arrangement.
The modulus or length of the 𝑝-th moment measures how strongly the data cluster when considered modulo 2 𝜋 𝑝 .
Across orders, a value of R𝑝 = 0 indicates complete uniformity around the circle.
R𝑝 = 1 corresponds to perfect alignment of the data wrapped onto a circle of length 2 𝜋 𝑝 , which has different implications for different values of 𝑝.
For 𝑝 = 1, this means all observations fall at the same angle, for 𝑝 = 2 they can be split between two opposite angles, and so forth.

While the argument and the modulus of the first circular moment describe central tendency and spread, higher-order circular moments allow us to characterize further aspects of a distribution's shape and symmetry.
We turn to these measures in the following sections.
Skewness describes the asymmetry or lopsidedness of a distribution.

In Euclidean statistics, a nonzero skewness statistic indicates that the data spread further from the mean in one direction than the other, with its sign corresponding to the direction of the long tail; it is calculated as the third moment of the 𝑧-scored (standardized) data.
Circular skewness extends this concept to periodic data, quantifying the asymmetry of a distribution around the circular mean.

Kurtosis describes how much probability mass lies in the tails of a distribution.
The Euclidean sample kurtosis b 2 is the fourth moment of the 𝑧-scored data.
As with skewness, 𝑧-scoring makes the kurtosis invariant to shifts or scaling of the data.
A Gaussian distribution has a kurtosis of 3, and as a result, the excess kurtosis of a sample in Euclidean space is defined as g2 = b 2 -3.
The distribution of a typical unimodal sample with positive excess kurtosis has a narrow peak around the mean and, extending away, heavier tails than the Gaussian distribution.
Conversely, the distribution of a sample with negative excess kurtosis is flatter and more spread out around the mean.

As in Euclidean statistics, an outlier in circular data is an observation that deviates markedly from others.
In behavioral and cognitive research, such values may reflect measurement errors, misunderstandings of the task, lapses in attention, or meaningful extreme values.
In circular statistics, detecting outliers requires special care because the ordering of the data is not unique and minimum and maximum values are not defined.
Outliers should be excluded sparingly to avoid biasing the results.
In this section, we briefly survey some methods for detecting outliers, from formal statistical tests to more algorithmic classification techniques.
One approach to detecting outliers in circular data is to use statistical goodness-of-fit tests that check whether the sample is drawn from an expected distribution.
These tests can be appropriate if researchers have clear expectations about the data's distribution based on previous empirical findings or theoretical considerations.
If the data deviate significantly from an expected distribution, this may indicate the presence of one or more outliers.
Resources on suitable tests are provided in Section Beyond This Tutorial.
While a significant result suggests the presence of outliers, statistical tests do not pinpoint which observations might be outliers.
Methods based on descriptive statistics identify outliers by analyzing how far each observation lies from a central value.

For example, outliers are sometimes defined as values that deviate from the mean by at least three standard deviations.
Analogously, extreme values in circular space can be excluded using a cutoff of a maximum deviation from the circular mean in terms of circular standard deviations.
However, outlier values can distort the circular mean and inflate the circular standard deviation.
Therefore, alternative outlier classification methods use measures that are more robust against influences from outliers.
The median absolute deviation is a robust measure of spread that can be used together with the circular median to identify outliers in circular data.
It is calculated by computing the angular distance of each observation from the circular median, and then calculating the Euclidean median of those distances.
Outliers can now be defined as values that deviate from the circular median by the median absolute deviation multiplied by some factor (e.g., three).
While methods based on distance and deviation provide an intuitive approach toward identifying concrete outlier candidates, they are sometimes criticized for being exploratory and subjective.
Another approach to detecting outliers is to identify patterns in the total data, rather than comparing individual data points to the overall summary.
These methods usually employ clustering and density-based algorithms.
Clustering algorithms structure data into subsets, aiming for high similarity between data points in one cluster and low similarity between data points of different clusters.
If most of the data form one large cluster and a few points form one or several tiny separate clusters, those few points can be deemed outliers.
For circular clustering algorithms, see Section Beyond This Tutorial.
While these methods allow for identifying multiple concrete outlier candidates, their results depend on the choice of the algorithm and hyperparameters.
In this section, we introduce probabilistic foundations and modeling approaches for random variables in a circular space.
The distribution of a circular random variable can be modeled by a probability density function (PDF) in a similar way to a Euclidean variable.
The key difference is that a circular PDF must be periodic, such that 𝑓 (𝜃) = 𝑓 (𝜃 + 2𝜋𝑘) for any integer 𝑘.
While a PDF in R 1 has integral ("area under the curve") equal to one over the whole real line (-∞, ∞), a valid PDF in circular space must integrate to 1 over any interval of length 2𝜋.

The CDF can be constructed over any interval of length 2𝜋; thus, the choice of starting point 𝜃 0 is an essential part of its specification.

In this section, we will outline population counterparts of the sample statistics discussed in Section Descriptive Statistics of Circular Data, address the conditions for sample-topopulation convergence in circular space, and describe some common circular population distributions.
We will compare two circular analogs of the Gaussian distribution and introduce two more flexible families for fitting heavy-tailed and skewed data.

We will examine the properties of circular random variables in more detail before concluding with practical guidelines for choosing between circular distributions and sampling random values from circular distributions.

The circular median discussed in Section Circular Median is not moment-based.

Like the sample version, the population circular median 𝜇 med can be defined in two ways: first, as an angle that divides the circle into two semicircles (𝜇 med -𝜋, 𝜇 med ) and (𝜇 med , 𝜇 med + 𝜋) that each contain equal probability mass of 1 2 ; second, as an angle that minimizes the expected circular distance from the random variable,
As for the sample case, the first definition yields at least two possible solutions; therefore, the second one should be preferred.
Note, however, that for certain distributions, the circular population median is not uniquely defined, even under the second definition (e.g., for symmetric, bi-, or multimodal distributions).
The properties and approximations for concentrated data described for sample statistics in the preceding section all generalize to their population counterparts.

The trigonometric moments of an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sample, including the mean resultant vector, converge to their population counterparts as the sample size increases (see Section Central Limit Theorem).

As a result, sample statistics that are continuous functions of the mean resultant vector (circular mean, variance, and standard deviation) and of higher-order trigonometric moments (circular skewness and kurtosis) inherit convergence via the continuous mapping theorem.
The only case where convergence of these parameters is not assured is when the true parameter is not uniquely defined.

For example, although we can calculate the circular mean of a sample drawn from the circular uniform distribution, the population mean resultant vector has length 0, so the mean direction is undefined and the sample mean direction has no population counterpart to converge to.
For parameters that are not moment-based, the question of convergence is more complicated.

The circular median also converges when the true value is uniquely defined and the density around it is well-behaved, that is, continuous and sufficiently smooth (for a detailed discussion, see Purkayastha, 1995).

text.text: One approach to modeling circular data is to "wrap" a Euclidean distribution around the circle to construct a wrapped distribution.

For a Euclidean distribution with PDF 𝑓 (𝑥), the result of wrapping is a circular PDF that can be written as the periodic sum 𝑓 W (𝜃) = ∑︁ ∞ 𝑘=-∞ 𝑓 (𝜃 + 2𝜋𝑘), where the sum is taken over all integers 𝑘 ∈ Z. Conveniently, the circular moments of the wrapped distribution are equal to the characteristic function of the unwrapped distribution evaluated at integer arguments, for example., the resultant vector (first circular moment) of a wrapped distribution is given by m1 = 𝜑(1), where 𝜑(𝑡) = E[𝑒 i𝑡 𝑥 ] is the characteristic function of the unwrapped distribution 𝑓 (𝑥).
The characteristic function also provides an alternative formulation of the PDF as a Fourier series, which is an infinite sum of sinusoidal components:
In practice, the infinite Fourier representation of a wrapped distribution cannot be evaluated exactly and must be approximated by truncating the series to a finite number of terms.
This means evaluating the characteristic function at a limited set of integer points, which produces a smooth approximation of the true circular PDF.
The resulting approximation is a finite Fourier series, and its accuracy improves as more terms are included.

The circular uniform distribution has the maximum entropy of any circular distribution.

The normal or Gaussian distribution family is fundamental in Euclidean space, underpinning many statistical models due to its well-behaved mathematical properties, including closed-form expression, defined moments, and closure under translation, convolution, and scaling.
For circular variables, no single family of distributions possesses all the desirable properties of the Gaussian, and some of its properties are not shared by any family of circular distributions.
The closest circular equivalents to the Gaussian are the wrapped normal distribution and the von Mises distribution (sometimes referred to as the circular normal).

The von Mises is a member of the exponential family of distributions, making it particularly suitable for statistical inference.

In fact, Richard von Mises originally derived the distribution named after him as that distribution for which the sample circular mean is the MLE of location, in the same way as the sample mean is the MLE for the location parameter of the Gaussian (von Mises, 1918).

text.text: The von Mises distribution can also be derived from a bivariate Gaussian distribution in the real plane R² .

The von Mises PDF is equal to the conditional density of polar angle 𝜃 given unit radial distance 𝑝(𝜃|𝑟 = 1) for a bivariate normal random variable with mean on the unit circle, at [cos 𝜇, sin 𝜇], equal variances 1 𝜅 and zero correlation.

This approach can be extended to define analogs of the von Mises in higher dimensions, known as von Mises-Fisher distributions: the von Mises-Fisher PDF in S 𝑝 is proportional to the restriction of an isotropic multivariate Gaussian distribution in R 𝑝+1 to the unit 𝑝-dimensional hypersphere.

Yet another way to obtain the von Mises distribution is as the hitting point on the unit circle of a two-dimensional Brownian diffusion (i.e., an accumulation of isotropic Gaussian noise) with constant drift in direction 𝜇 with velocity 𝜅 (Gordon & Hudson, 1977).

text.text: Unlike the wrapped normal PDF, which involves an infinite sum of Gaussian densities, the PDF of the von Mises distribution has an analytic expression, as do some key quantities such as Fisher information and entropy (most of these involve Bessel functions, but most mathematical software packages have built-in functions for their efficient numerical approximation).

A family of distributions is closed under convolution if the sum of two independent random variables from that family also belongs to the same family (the PDF of the sum is obtained by applying the mathematical operation of convolution to the PDFs of the two variables).
The wrapped normal inherits closure under convolution from its Euclidean counterpart, the Gaussian (Section Sampling Distribution of the Circular Mean below).
However, a number of other properties that make the Gaussian distribution special are instead possessed by the von Mises distribution in circular space.
Like the Gaussian, the von Mises is a maximum entropy distribution.
Specifically, among all distributions on the circle with a given circular mean and variance (or equivalently, a given mean resultant vector), the von Mises distribution has the maximum entropy.
More similarities and differences between these distributions are described in Section General Properties of Circular Random Variables.

We next introduce two families of distributions that can serve as flexible models for circular data that are asymmetric or heavy-tailed.
Both are four-parameter families of distributions varying in tailedness and skewness as well as location and scale.
The wrapped stable family generalizes the wrapped normal distribution and retains the property of closure under convolution, meaning that sums of random variables belong to the same family.
The sine-skewed Jones-Pewsey family generalizes the von Mises distribution and its PDF has an analytic expression based on trigonometric functions.
Particular attention will be given to the wrapped Cauchy distribution, which uniquely belongs to both families.
A distribution is called stable if linear combinations of random variables have the same distribution up to location and scale.
In Euclidean space, stable distributions are important as they generalize the concept of a central limit distribution (Section Central Limit Theorem) to include distributions with nonfinite variance.
In a circular space all continuous distributions have finite variance, but wrapping the stable family provides a flexible model for skewed and heavy-tailed data that is also closed under convolution.

Models of Euclidean random variables often make use of properties of the mean and variance, such as additivity, that do not apply or apply differently in circular spaces.

The Euclidean mean or expectation is additive in the sense that the mean of the sum of any two random variables is equal to the sum of their means, and Euclidean variance is additive in the sense that the variance of the sum of two random variables is equal to the sum of their variances, so long as the variables are uncorrelated,
These properties are key to understanding how variability from different sources combines and how random noise accumulates (e.g., in drift-diffusion models; Bogacz et al., 2006; Ratcliff, 1978).

The central limit theorem (CLT) states that, under quite general conditions, the sum or mean of a sample of Euclidean random variables converges to a normal (Gaussian) distribution as the number of observations in the sample grows, even if the individual observations do not come from a normal distribution.

This fact is often called upon to justify the use of the normal distribution family as a default model for a wide range of behavioral and neural observations, and also underlies many parametric statistical tests.
Analogous results to the CLT for circular variables are therefore of considerable interest; however, the topic is complex.
In circular spaces, the limiting distribution depends on precisely what operation is performed on the random variables.

It should be plain that the angular sum of increasingly many independent circular random variables, regardless of their individual distributions, will in general grow in dispersion and ultimately converge to the circular uniform distribution.
Of more interest is the limiting distribution of the mean resultant vector, the direction of which is the closest circular analog of the Euclidean mean.

For i.i.d. circular variables, the mean resultant vector converges to a bivariate Gaussian centered on the mean resultant vector of the distribution they are sampled from, and with covariance that can be calculated from its first two circular moments (Jammalamadaka & SenGupta, 2001, Section 3.4).

text.text: In particular, if that distribution is symmetrical, the bivariate Gaussian is uncorrelated, so the tangent of the resultant direction converges to a Gaussian distribution.

If the distribution of resultant direction is narrow enough (which it will be for sufficiently large numbers of samples, as long as they are not uniformly distributed), then it will have approximately the same distribution as its tangent.
Based on this, we can deduce that the limiting distribution of the circular mean of symmetrically distributed circular random variables is approximately Gaussian in shape.
Unfortunately, this is not sufficient to identify a specific circular distribution.

In particular, both wrapped normal and von Mises PDFs converge to Gaussian as their width approaches 0, so we cannot identify either of these circular analogs of the Gaussian as the unique limiting distribution.

text.text: After being introduced to a range of established circular distribution families and their properties, the reader should now be able to choose suitable distributions when building statistical models of circular data.
If the data come from a source with no directional bias, the circular uniform distribution should be used.

If not, two criteria can be employed for selecting one of the distribution families discussed above: first, whether the data can be expected to have an approximately normal distribution; second, whether the purposes of analysis better suit the properties of wrapped distributions or those defined intrinsically on the circle.

If a normal distribution can be assumed (based on inspection or because the conditions described in Section Central Limit Theorem are met), then the von Mises or the wrapped normal is appropriate; if not, and assuming the data are nonetheless approximately unimodal, the Jones-Pewsey or wrapped stable should be chosen for their ability to capture asymmetry and tailedness of data.

Wrapped distribution families are more appropriate for data obtained by wrapping Euclidean random variables or when the analysis involves addition or subtraction of circular variables (because these families are closed under convolution).

Distributions that are defined intrinsically on the circle are appropriate if the reader needs an analytically and computationally tractable model for statistical inference, such as MLE or Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, or if they want a closed-form PDF, entropy or Fisher information.

If theoretical and practical considerations do not identify a single distribution family, we recommend selecting based on how well the different possible distributions fit the data, noting, however, that differences in fit between wrapped and intrinsically circular distributions are typically small.
Sampling from circular distributions is essential for generating synthetic data and experimental stimuli and for use in simulations and model recovery.
For wrapped distributions, the usual method is to draw samples from the corresponding distribution in Euclidean space and then wrap the generated random values onto the circle.
Distributions that are defined intrinsically on the circle require different sampling methods.
For the von Mises distribution, the rejection sampling algorithm introduced by Best and Fisher (1979) has become the standard.

text.text: More generally, inverse transform sampling provides a universal framework for generating random variables from any continuous distribution with a known CDF: generate a random value 𝑈 from a uniform distribution in the interval [0, 1], and return the smallest number 𝑋 for which 𝐹 (𝑋) ≥ 𝑈, where 𝐹 is the CDF of the target distribution.
This method can be used for sampling from circular distributions with the CDF defined over any specified interval of length 2𝜋.

text.text: First, this algorithm computes the total free length available after enforcing the minimum spacing requirement.
It then samples 𝑁 random values within this remaining space.
After sorting the samples, a minimum separation of at least minDistance of adjacent values is ensured by applying a cumulative offset of (𝑖 -1) × minDistance.
Optionally, the original order of the values can be restored -for instance, when experimental stimuli are presented sequentially and should not appear in a sorted order.
Finally, the list of values is rotated by a random offset and wrapped back onto the circular range, yielding a uniform random arrangement of points while ensuring the specified minimum separation.
The separation constraints and the maximum number of samples are inversely related: for a minimum separation distance Δ 𝑚𝑖𝑛 , the number of samples 𝑛 is constrained by 𝑛 ≤ ⌊︂ 𝑅 Δ min .

Once the separation constraints are specified, angular distance (Section Measuring Distance) can be computed pairwise to all data points to verify that every pair of circular observations meets the requirements.
In Equation 41, the normalizing constant of the Jones-Pewsey distribution is expressed as an associated Legendre function, which becomes numerically unstable when 𝜓 is large and negative.
The algorithm below avoids this by computing the density using numerical integration of the kernel and working in log space to prevent floating-point overflow.
When 𝜓 = 0, the distribution reduces to the von Mises and its analytic normalizing constant is used instead.

The Euclidean mean or expectation is additive in the sense that the mean of the sum of any two random variables is equal to the sum of their means, and Euclidean variance is additive in the sense that the variance of the sum of two random variables is equal to the sum of their variances, so long as the variables are uncorrelated,

Circular equivalents to mean and variance are related to the direction and length of the mean resultant vector, which for the angular sum of two variables 𝜃 and 𝜙 is given by that is, the mean resultant vector of the sum of two independent random angles is the product of their individual mean resultant vectors.
We confine ourselves now to the case of independent 𝜃 and 𝜙.
The circular mean is the direction or argument of the mean resultant vector, using arg(𝑧 1 𝑧 2 ) = arg 𝑧 1 + arg 𝑧 2 for any complex 𝑧 1 , 𝑧 2 .
In other words, the circular mean is additive for independent variables.
Circular measures of dispersion are related to the mean resultant length, using |𝑧 1 𝑧 2 | = |𝑧 1 ||𝑧 2 | for any complex 𝑧 1 , 𝑧 2 .
In other words, the mean resultant length does not have the additive property, and by extension neither does the circular variance, based on its usual definition 𝑉 𝜃 = 1 -𝜌.
However, log 𝜌[𝜃 + 𝜙] = log 𝜌[𝜃] + log 𝜌[𝜙] that is, the logarithm of mean resultant length is additive for independent circular random variables.
Based on the definition of circular standard deviation, it follows that squared circular standard deviation is also additive for independent variables,
